questions.q: Training error is tiny but validation error is much higher. What does this gap indicate?
options: Underfitting: the model is too simple
Overfitting: the model is fitting noise in the training data
The ideal model: low training error is all that matters
The validation set must be broken
questions.explain: When a model fits training data much better than held-out data, the gap is evidence of overfitting: the extra flexibility wiggles between (and beyond) the training points.

questions.q: As you raise the polynomial degree, what happens to the **training** error (exact least squares, nested models)?
questions.explain: A higher-degree polynomial can always reproduce a lower-degree fit (set the extra coefficients to 0), so its best training error is at most as large. It is the *validation* error that often forms a U-shape.

questions.q: The data noise level is $\sigma = 0.5$. What is the lowest expected MSE even the **true** hidden pattern would achieve on new data?
questions.explain: The noise is irreducible: even a perfect model has expected MSE $\sigma^2 = 0.5^2 = 0.25$. A validation MSE far below $\sigma^2$ on a fresh sample would be suspicious.

questions.q: Why does the page report a separate **test** MSE after choosing the degree on the validation set?
options: The test set is larger, so its error is always lower
The validation error is computed on training data
The validation error influenced the choice, so it tends to be optimistic; an untouched test set gives a fair estimate
To pick the degree a second time
questions.explain: Selecting the best of many validation scores biases that score downward. The test set is looked at once; if you kept tuning on it, it would become a second validation set.
